drake.bio: Toronto-born rapper, singer, songwriter and actor Aubrey Drake Graham moved from a teenage role on Degrassi: The Next Generation into one of the defining careers of the streaming era. His 2009 breakout “Best I Ever Had” was followed by the chart-topping debut Thank Me Later and the 2011 album Take Care, which won the GRAMMY for Best Rap Album and helped cement his blend of rap, melodic R&B and emotionally direct songwriting. Over the next decade, projects including Nothing Was the Same, Views and Scorpion expanded that sound while hits such as “Hotline Bling,” “God’s Plan” and “One Dance” made him a dominant global chart presence. Drake’s success also changed how Toronto was heard internationally: his music, OVO imprint and collaborations with local producers and artists helped turn the city into a major centre of contemporary rap and R&B. His combination of singing and rapping, diaristic writing and internet-era release strategy has influenced a generation of artists well beyond Canada.

justin bieber.bio: London, Ontario-born and Stratford-raised singer Justin Bieber became one of the first global pop superstars to emerge directly from social media. Videos of his performances posted online led to his discovery as a teenager, and the 2009 EP My World introduced him to an international audience. His 2010 debut album My World 2.0 reached No. 1 in the United States and produced “Baby,” establishing Bieber as a defining teen-pop figure of the early 2010s. He later broadened his sound through electronic, R&B and dance-pop collaborations, especially on Purpose, which included “Sorry,” “What Do You Mean?” and “Love Yourself.” His work with Skrillex and Diplo on “Where Are Ü Now” earned his first GRAMMY, while later albums such as Changes, Justice and 2025’s SWAG showed an increasingly R&B-oriented approach. Bieber’s path from small-town Ontario performer to worldwide pop star became a template for online artist discovery, and his longevity has made him one of the most internationally visible Canadian artists of his generation.

alanis morissette.bio: Ottawa-born singer-songwriter Alanis Morissette began her recording career in Canada as a teenage pop artist before radically reinventing her sound with 1995’s Jagged Little Pill. Created with producer Glen Ballard, the album paired conversational, confessional writing with alternative rock and became an international phenomenon through songs including “You Oughta Know,” “Hand in My Pocket,” “Ironic” and “You Learn.” It reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and won Album of the Year and Best Rock Album at the GRAMMY Awards, while “You Oughta Know” won Best Rock Song and Best Female Rock Vocal Performance. The record’s frank treatment of anger, intimacy, spirituality and self-examination helped expand the emotional vocabulary available to women in mainstream rock and influenced generations of singer-songwriters who followed. Morissette continued exploring alternative rock, electronic textures and introspective songwriting on albums including Supposed Former Infatuation Junkie and Under Rug Swept. Her career remains one of the clearest examples of a Canadian artist reshaping global popular music while maintaining an unmistakably personal writing voice.

kardinal offishall.bio: Toronto rapper, songwriter, producer, DJ and music executive Kardinal Offishall is one of the foundational figures in Canadian hip-hop. Emerging from Toronto’s 1990s rap scene, he developed a distinctly local sound that fused hip-hop with the reggae and dancehall traditions of the city’s Caribbean communities. Early releases such as Eye & I and Quest for Fire: Firestarter, Vol. 1 helped establish him as a major Canadian voice, while “BaKardi Slang” became an enduring statement of Toronto identity and vocabulary. His international breakthrough came with the Akon-assisted “Dangerous,” bringing a Canadian rap artist rare mainstream visibility at the time. Beyond his own catalogue, Kardinal has consistently championed Canadian talent through collaborations, mentorship, executive work and public advocacy for the country’s hip-hop history. Canada’s Walk of Fame honoured him with the Allan Slaight Music Impact Honour in 2023. His importance is larger than any single hit: he helped build the bridge between the pre-global era of Toronto rap and the generation that later made the city an international hip-hop centre.

the weeknd.bio: Scarborough-born singer-songwriter and producer Abel Tesfaye transformed the sound of contemporary R&B under the name The Weeknd. He first attracted attention anonymously in 2011 with dark, atmospheric songs released online and collected on the mixtape House of Balloons, whose hazy production and emotionally detached writing helped shape the emerging alternative-R&B movement. After the mixtape trilogy and 2013 debut album Kiss Land, he moved into global pop without abandoning that darker aesthetic. Beauty Behind the Madness, Starboy and After Hours produced major hits including “Can’t Feel My Face,” “Starboy” and “Blinding Lights,” while his cinematic visuals and recurring characters turned albums into larger narrative worlds. Tesfaye has won multiple GRAMMY Awards, headlined the Super Bowl halftime show and expanded into film and television. His 2025 album Hurry Up Tomorrow continued the long-running artistic arc associated with The Weeknd persona. From anonymous Toronto uploads to stadium-scale pop, his career helped make the city’s moody R&B vocabulary globally influential and established him as one of Canada’s most consequential 21st-century artists.

céline dion.bio: Charlemagne, Québec-born singer Céline Dion built one of the most successful international careers ever achieved by a Canadian artist. She began recording in French as a teenager and was already a major star in Québec before winning the 1988 Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland. Her 1990 English-language debut Unison opened the North American market, and the duet “Beauty and the Beast” with Peabo Bryson earned her first GRAMMY. Through the 1990s, albums such as The Colour of My Love, Falling into You and Let’s Talk About Love established Dion as a defining voice of adult contemporary pop. “My Heart Will Go On,” the theme from Titanic, became her signature global hit and won Record of the Year at the GRAMMY Awards. Dion’s career is also notable for sustained success in both French and English and for helping normalize large-scale Las Vegas residencies for contemporary pop stars. Her technical control, dramatic delivery and international reach made her a model for generations of powerhouse vocalists and one of Québec and Canada’s most recognizable cultural exports.

shania twain.bio: Raised in Timmins, Ontario, Shania Twain became the central crossover figure in 1990s country-pop and one of Canada’s most commercially successful artists. After an early country debut, she found her breakthrough with 1995’s The Woman in Me, whose polished production and assertive songwriting broadened her audience far beyond traditional country radio. She expanded that formula on 1997’s Come On Over, a landmark album driven by songs including “You’re Still the One,” “That Don’t Impress Me Much” and “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” The record’s blend of country instrumentation, pop hooks and rock-scale production helped reshape the commercial possibilities of the genre, while Twain’s songwriting and visual identity made her a model for later crossover stars. She has won five GRAMMY Awards and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 2011. After health problems interrupted her performing career, Twain returned to recording and touring, reinforcing a legacy that extends well beyond sales: she helped establish a modern blueprint for artists moving fluidly between country and global pop.

avril lavigne.bio: Ontario singer-songwriter Avril Lavigne emerged in 2002 as a teenage alternative to the highly polished pop dominating the era. Raised in Greater Napanee, she broke internationally with Let Go, an album built around guitar-driven songs such as “Complicated,” “Sk8er Boi” and “I’m with You.” Its mix of pop melody, skate-punk attitude and confessional songwriting earned multiple GRAMMY nominations and made Lavigne a defining figure in the early-2000s pop-punk boom. She followed with the darker Under My Skin and later moved between pop-rock, power pop and more overtly commercial pop while retaining the directness and rebellious visual language associated with her debut. Her influence became especially visible during the pop-punk revival of the early 2020s, when a new generation of artists cited the style she helped bring into mainstream pop. Lavigne returned emphatically to the genre with 2022’s Love Sux and celebrated more than two decades of work with a Greatest Hits project and tour. Her career helped open mainstream space for young women using punk aesthetics without abandoning pop songwriting.

bryan adams.bio: Kingston-born singer-songwriter, guitarist and photographer Bryan Adams became one of Canada’s most durable international rock stars through a catalogue built on direct melodies, raspy vocals and arena-sized choruses. After early records established his partnership with songwriter Jim Vallance, 1983’s Cuts Like a Knife brought wider recognition and 1984’s Reckless turned Adams into a global star. The album produced a run of enduring singles including “Run to You,” “Summer of ’69,” “Heaven” and the Tina Turner duet “It’s Only Love.” He later became closely associated with film soundtracks, most notably the worldwide hit “(Everything I Do) I Do It for You” from Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves, as well as “All for Love” with Rod Stewart and Sting. Adams has also written for other artists and maintained parallel work as a professional photographer. His decades-long touring career and international catalogue made him one of the Canadian performers who helped establish a reliable global market for homegrown rock music before the streaming era.

sarah mclachlan.bio: Halifax-born singer-songwriter Sarah McLachlan became one of the defining Canadian voices of 1990s adult alternative and singer-songwriter pop. After relocating to Vancouver and signing with Nettwerk, she developed a spacious, emotionally direct style on albums including Touch, Solace and Fumbling Towards Ecstasy. Her international breakthrough deepened with 1997’s Surfacing, which included “Building a Mystery,” “Adia” and “Angel” and established her as a major crossover artist. McLachlan’s influence extends beyond her own catalogue. She co-founded Lilith Fair, the late-1990s touring festival built around women artists at a time when promoters and radio programmers often treated female performers as competing for limited space. The festival became both a commercial success and an important platform for women across pop, rock, folk and alternative music. McLachlan has won multiple JUNO and GRAMMY Awards and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame in 2017. Her combination of introspective songwriting, atmospheric production and institution-building gives her a lasting place in Canadian music history beyond the ballads for which she is best known.
